blocks.text: Hosea’s references to Gibeah and Jacob belong to a broader, disputed reading in which the book reuses memories of the exodus, wilderness, Baal-peor, and earlier prophetic traditions to diagnose Israel’s present identity and call for change. The chapter’s warnings about Samaria, its king, and Assyria also look toward Samaria’s fall as a major historical horizon. That horizon should not be dated too simply: the often-cited dates 722/721 and Sargon II’s consolidation in 720 refer to distinguishable moments. Assyrian royal inscriptions can help place such campaigns in view, but they are imperial self-presentations rather than neutral confirmation of every detail in Hosea.
